title: REVIEW: A second Tartuffe has hit NYC, but this one doesn’t quite liv...
transcript: It is hard to think of a show currently playing in New York City with a more stacked cast and creative team than Tartuffe, which is currently playing at the New York Theater Workshop. The cast is filled with film and TV stars of Broadway and off Broadway favorites. And then you have a script by Lucas Naith, who is a super talented playwright, along with music by Heather Christian, who is one of my favorite up and coming musical theater composers. And I think that the story of Tartuffe is one that could be incredibly relevant in today's day and age. Like, there's a reason why this is the second production of Tartuffe that we are getting in the past couple months. But unfortunately, I don't really think that this is a production that lived up to its full potential. And I do unfortunately think a lot of that is due to Matthew Broderick's casting as Tartuffe. I actually think that Matthew Broderick is an incredibly talented actor, and his, like, dry and awkward line delivery works really well in a show like the producers, but not really so much in a show like Tartuffe. Tartuffe is supposed to be this really enigmatic figure who David Cross's character becomes enamored by. Matthew Broderick plays the role so stoically that it's hard to imagine anyone really falling under his spell. That's such a core plot point to the show that if you don't believe that someone could fall for his bullshit, it Kind of starts to unravel the whole show. I also don't really think that this production had a clear sense of what it was trying to say. It ends with a musical moment of sorts, and it almost felt like the ending of a completely different show. I loved that moment in a Silo and what it was saying. It just didn't feel like it tracked with the rest of what we had seen before it. In fact, a lot of the elements of this production feel like they are from different productions. You have these instrumental moments between scenes with animal noises that seem to come out of nowhere. You have this tennis motif, with the set being designed to look like an old fashioned tennis court and the occasional tennis racket, but it's not really clear what tennis has to do with the story at all. And so what you're left with is this somewhat confused production that feels like it's throwing out a lot of different ideas, but it never quite gels together. I do think there is still a lot of fun to be had with seeing this particular group of actors on stage together. And even though I found Matthew Broderick's performance to be a bit lacking, I did think everyone else was pretty solid to really great. I just wish they had a better production to work with, because I think this could have been really great, but what we got was just kind Of meh
